title: Log
summary: git log lists the history of commits, newest first, with who made each one and why.

levels.title: Read the history
levels.briefing: git log walks back through the commits from where you are now. Each entry shows the commit's id, author, date and message. Add --oneline for a short version.
levels.objective: Write the number of commits in the history right now into answer.txt, then commit it.
hints: git log --oneline shows one line per commit. Count them.
There are 3. Put that number in answer.txt.
Run: echo 3 > answer.txt, git add answer.txt, git commit -m "Answer"
levels.successMessage: git log reads the chain of commits from HEAD backwards, so you can always count and inspect your history.

levels.title: Who started it?
levels.objective: Write the author name of the very first commit into who.txt, then commit it.
hints: The first commit is at the bottom of git log.
Run: echo Ada > who.txt, git add who.txt, git commit -m "Add author"
levels.successMessage: Every commit records its author, so the history shows who made each change.

levels.title: Same message
levels.objective: Make a new commit (any change) whose message is exactly the same as the first commit's message.
hints: Find the oldest commit in git log.
Make any change, stage it, and commit with that message.
Run: echo x > x.txt, git add x.txt, git commit -m "Start the project"
levels.successMessage: Commit messages are kept forever in the log, which is why clear messages matter.

levels.title: The latest message
levels.objective: Write the latest commit's message into last.txt, then commit it.
hints: git log -n 1 shows only the newest commit.
Run: echo "Update the menu" > last.txt, git add last.txt, git commit -m "Save message"
levels.successMessage: The newest commit is always at the top of git log.
